title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge that generative artificial intelligence poses for school mathematics, especially the risk that students can bypass interpretation, decision-making, and validation when tasks are easily solvable by AI. The author argues that in post-AI contexts, the central didactic issue is not the technology itself, but the kind of mathematical activity that classroom tasks elicit and how that activity is regulated.

To respond to this problem, the paper analyzes a classroom experience in secondary education where open mathematical tasks were implemented together with a didactic regulation device called COMPAS. COMPAS structures task work into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, modeling, exploring results, validating, and socializing conclusions. The study uses a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach and examines student written work, classroom interactions, and teacher-observer notes.

The paper focuses on a secondary school classroom in Peru and on students working on open-ended mathematics tasks designed so that no direct computational shortcut would be possible. The tasks intentionally lacked explicit numerical data and closed instructions, forcing students to interpret the situation, make assumptions, build models, and justify their choices, while using AI only as a subordinate support tool when appropriate.

The main conclusion is that, when task design and classroom regulation are explicit, students can retain epistemic control over mathematical activity even in the presence of generative AI. The study suggests that open tasks, combined with structured didactic mediation, preserve student agency, support meaningful modeling and validation, and prevent AI from replacing the formative core of mathematics learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative descriptive-interpretive classroom study with no control group, randomization, or quantitative effect estimation. It provides useful practice-based evidence but only meets limited credibility criteria for causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest positive instructional impact on mathematical participation and agency, but there are no measurable effect sizes or comparative outcomes. The impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude for general K-12 use.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI is used as an available support tool during secondary-school mathematics task solving, mainly to explore or contrast results rather than to deliver tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative secondary-school classroom experience, open mathematical tasks mediated by the COMPAS regulation device appeared to sustain students' mathematical activity and preserve epistemic control even with generative AI available. The study does not report quantitative effect sizes; it reports that students remained engaged in interpretation, modeling, and validation of solutions under explicit didactic regulation (n not reported).
finding.measure: Classroom observations, student written work, and interaction records focused on mathematical modeling, validation, and epistemic control

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that open tasks supported students' mathematical agency, decision-making, justification, and critical validation of AI-generated outputs. These are described qualitatively rather than measured with a statistic, and no sample size or effect size is reported (n not reported).
finding.measure: Observed agency, justification, negotiation of assumptions, and critical evaluation of AI outputs during classroom task resolution
